issue: Can a district court consider a nonretroactive change in sentencing law as an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i)?

sides.position: A nonretroactive change in sentencing law cannot, by itself or in combination with the defendant's individualized circumstances, be an extraordinary and compelling reason for compassionate release.
cases: United States v. Andrews, 12 F.4th 255 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Thacker, 4 F.4th 569 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Crandall, 25 F.4th 582 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Jenkins, 50 F.4th 1197 (10th Cir. 2022)
United States v. McCall, 56 F.4th 1048 (6th Cir. 2022)

sides.position: A nonretroactive change in law may be considered, in the context of the defendant's individualized circumstances, as part of the extraordinary-and-compelling analysis.
cases: United States v. Ruvalcaba, 26 F.4th 14 (1st Cir. 2022) (Barron, J., concurring)

this_court: The en banc majority holds that a nonretroactive change in law is not an extraordinary and compelling reason on its own; it aligns with the 3d, 7th, 8th, and 10th Circuits.
quote: The majority's decision puts us in conflict with these courts and further entrenches the circuit split on this issue.
cite: United States v. David McCall, Jr., 56 F.4th 1048 (6th Cir. 2022)
